strengths: The paper presents a clear and general SMC-sampler template for stochastic optimisation with intractable gradients, with Algorithm 1 and the ULA special case described explicitly.
It usefully unifies existing methods such as JALA-EM (Cuin et al., 2025) and the EBM SMC sampler of Carbone et al. (2024) as special cases, and it highlights flexibility in kernel choices.
The empirical study on reward tuning of Langevin processes, 2D EBMs, and MNIST is reasonably detailed, with many hyperparameters and implementation choices reported in the appendix.
The authors are transparent about limitations, explicitly deferring particle-level theoretical analysis to future work and noting evaluation caveats.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely trivial or idealised. Theorem 1 is the standard Feynman-Kac identity, Lemma 1 is an immediate exact-expectation recovery result, and Proposition 2 reduces to exact gradient descent under PL conditions. There is no convergence, bias, or MSE guarantee for the actual SMC particle approximation; the paper explicitly leaves this to future work, so the claimed theoretical soundness of SOSMC is not substantiated.

The ESS analysis is limited to a Gaussian toy example and local chi-square expansions. The appendix proofs contain errors and inconsistencies (e.g., Proposition 5 appears to lose a square in the chi-square scaling, Proposition numbering is mismatched, and notation is inconsistent), and the analysis does not cover resampling or practical ESS behaviour in the full algorithm.

Novelty is modest. The framework is an application of standard SMC samplers, and the ULA-based instantiation recovers existing algorithms from Cuin et al. (2025) and Carbone et al. (2024). The main new element is applying importance weighting in reward-tuning settings rather than a fundamentally new particle method.

The empirical evaluation is insufficient to support the broad claims. Only reward tuning is tested, despite maximum marginal likelihood and latent-variable models being primary motivating applications. The main comparison is to ImpDiff and SOUL, but the most relevant SMC baseline (Carbone et al., 2024) is not compared against even though it is a special case of the proposed framework.

Efficiency claims are mixed. Appendix E.1 admits IMPDIFF is fastest per outer iteration because SOSMC requires extra gradient evaluations and weight bookkeeping. Wall-clock gains are demonstrated mainly in a low-dimensional setup, while the MNIST experiment is qualitative and lacks wall-clock or KL evaluation.

Presentation and reproducibility have issues: no code release is mentioned, and the manuscript contains equation inconsistencies (e.g., objective signs in Eq. 20 vs. Eq. 28), duplicate or incorrect figure captions, and several typos that make the work harder to build on.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: stochastic optimisation when gradients are intractable expectations over parameter-dependent distributions.

Provides a general SMC-sampler framework that unifies existing ULA-based methods such as JALA-EM (Cuin et al., 2025) and the SMC EBM training scheme of Carbone et al. (2024) as special cases, offering some conceptual clarity.

Derives gradient estimators for reward tuning of EBMs under both forward- and reverse-KL regularisation, and includes detailed experimental protocols such as device-synchronised wall-clock timing and fresh-chain evaluation.
Includes local theoretical derivations for ESS and chi-square divergence between consecutive targets, illustrating sensitivity to step size and gradient norm.
Experiments cover a controlled Langevin-process setting, 2D EBM reward tuning, and MNIST EBM reward tuning, with multiple baselines and several random seeds in some settings.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially standard SMC samplers applied to stochastic optimisation. The main technical advance over prior work is replacing inner MCMC loops with SMC approximations, but this is already the core of existing special cases, and the added generality is mostly a choice of forward/backward kernels.

The theoretical analysis does not support the actual particle-based algorithm. Lemma 1 and Proposition 2 analyse an idealised recursion with exact expectations, which reduces to exact gradient descent. No convergence rate or finite-particle guarantee is provided for the practical SOSMC scheme; the authors explicitly leave this to future work. Thus the central claim of theoretical soundness for the proposed method is unsupported.

The ESS analysis is local and heuristic. It does not establish global behaviour or guarantees for the algorithm-dependent target sequence, and the proposed adaptive step-size rule is motivated only by this local approximation.

Experimental evidence is limited and mixed. The paper only tests reward tuning of EBMs, despite also motivating MMLE and EBM training. It compares against only IMPDIFF and SOUL, not against the existing SMC methods that are special cases (e.g., Carbone et al., 2024), nor against other strong baselines such as PCD with fresh sampling.

Claims of significant computational gains are not uniformly supported. Appendix E.1 states that IMPDIFF is consistently the fastest method in wall-clock per iteration, while SOSMC requires two gradient evaluations per outer iteration plus weight bookkeeping. Improvements are sometimes modest or comparable, especially for large beta_KL.

The 2D EBM comparison focuses on outer iterations rather than wall-clock time because IMPDIFF needs long evaluation chains. This may favour SOSMC and does not clearly establish computational efficiency. The MNIST experiment reports mainly qualitative samples and lacks quantitative objective/reward numbers.

Presentation and reproducibility are weak. Algorithm 1 contains errors (e.g., missing superscript in the weight update, nonsensical 'Set X_k^(i)=X_k^(i)'), Proposition 2 cites a non-existent 'Proposition 1', figure numbering and references are inconsistent, and several citations are malformed. No code release or reproducibility statement is provided.

No explicit limitations section. The paper does not adequately discuss failure modes, computational overhead, weight degeneracy, or settings where SOSMC is expected to underperform. Ethical implications of reward tuning generative models are also not discussed.

strengths: Provides a general SMC-based framework for stochastic optimisation with intractable gradients, and shows that existing methods such as JALA-EM and the SMC sampler of Carbone et al. arise as special cases through ULA forward/backward kernels.

The Feynman-Kac identity for gradient estimation and the SOSMC algorithm are clearly presented, with the weighted particle estimator offering a principled way to correct for non-equilibrium particle distributions.
The paper gives useful practical insights via ESS analysis, including the effect of step-size and gradient magnitude on weight degeneracy, and proposes a simple ESS-based step-size adaptation scheme.

Experiments on reward tuning of Langevin processes and EBMs (2D and MNIST) show that SOSMC-ULA can converge faster and achieve better objective values than IMPDIFF in several settings, with weighted particle rewards tracking fresh rewards more closely than unweighted averages.
The authors are honest about the limitations of the theoretical analysis, explicitly leaving convergence of the particle approximation and detailed SMC analysis to future work.
The framework is flexible and suggests how to incorporate alternative forward/backward kernels, which may be valuable for designing problem-specific optimisation samplers.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are limited to an idealised scheme where the Feynman-Kac expectations are computed exactly; Proposition 2 then reduces to standard gradient descent and does not analyse the actual particle-based algorithm. No convergence, bias, or MSE guarantees are provided for the implemented stochastic method despite the introduction claiming a theoretically sound framework.

The target sequence \pi_{\theta_k} is adaptive and depends on the particle system through the parameter updates. This feedback loop is not accounted for in the Feynman-Kac identity or the importance weights, so the standard SMC unbiasedness argument does not directly apply. The paper acknowledges this in Remark 4 but does not resolve the resulting theoretical gap.

The efficiency claims are only partially supported. Appendix E.1 notes that IMPDIFF is often faster per outer iteration because SOSMC requires additional gradient evaluations and weight bookkeeping, and wall-clock gains are not consistently demonstrated across settings.

The experimental evaluation is narrow: all experiments are reward tuning of EBMs or Langevin processes, while the framework is motivated by broader applications such as maximum marginal likelihood estimation and EBM training. No experiments are provided for those settings.

Baselines are limited mainly to IMPDIFF and SOUL. There is no comparison to standard inner-loop MCMC gradient estimators, PCD-style methods, or existing SMC-EM/JALA-EM approaches, making it difficult to judge the practical advantage over established alternatives.
The ESS analysis relies on simple Gaussian or local Taylor-expansion arguments, which may not capture the global behaviour of weight degeneracy in complex, high-dimensional, or multimodal targets.
Reproducibility could be improved: no code release or data generation scripts are mentioned, and while appendices provide hyperparameters, exact reproduction of the experiments may be challenging.

Presentation is dense and contains some minor notational and pseudocode issues (e.g., Algorithm 1 formatting and indexing), and there is no explicit limitations or broader-impact discussion beyond future-work remarks.
